prompt.context: Your client is the American Liquor Sales House (ALSH), an international company known for selling unique and prized wines. ALSH is concerned about their declining profitability over the past few years and have requested our help to figure out why and what they should do.
prompt.question: What is causing ALSH's profitability issue?

clarifying_info.q: Does ALSH have a physical presence?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, it has a few stores in major cities in the US, but the bulk of its sales occur online.
No – aim to increase as much as possible.
Internationally – mainly to private collectors and enthusiasts.

exhibits.title: Likelihood of a Wine Being Fake
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the percentage likelihood that a bottle is counterfeit for each wine size: Magnum, Liter, and Standard.

data.note: Cost of refund and credit is $200

framework: 1. ALSH (internal): a) Revenue – number of bottles sold, price per bottle; b) Costs – fixed costs (advertising, online platform maintenance, warehouse/store rent), variable costs (cost of wines sold, shipping); c) Reputation / demand for products

2. Wine market (external): a) Competitors – fragmented/consolidated, market share; b) Customers – changes in preferences, demographics; c) Regulatory issues – licenses required for exporting alcohol internationally
3. Opportunities: a) Exclusive partnerships with vineyards; b) Expansion to non-alcoholic beverages

questions.prompt: How profitable is ALSH? Calculate total annual profit.
questions.guidance: Ask the candidate what data they need. Provide: annual expenses of $34.5m; wine size table with number sold, price, and cost. Strong answer calculates contribution per size, sums gross profit, then subtracts fixed costs.

math.setup: Gross profit per size = (Price – Cost) x Number sold. Total profit = sum of gross profits – annual expenses.

questions.prompt: ALSH has been unknowingly selling fake wines. How much do fake wines cost ALSH? (Provide Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 1 fake-rate percentages, apply to number sold per size, multiply by $200 refund, and multiply by 50% detection rate (only 50% of fakes are caught and refunded). Strong answer builds a table and totals all refunds.

math.setup: Total refunds per size = Number sold x Fake rate x Refund amount x Detection rate (50%). Then sum across sizes.
math.answer: Fake wines cost ALSH $2.1m in refunds; revised net profit is $18.4m

questions.prompt: A third party can screen all wines to eliminate fakes. What is the maximum flat rate per bottle ALSH should be willing to pay for screening?
questions.guidance: Two thresholds to find: (1) breakeven vs. current (with fakes) profit of $18.4m; (2) breakeven vs. zero profit. At $0.30/bottle, screening cost equals current refund cost ($2.1m) so profit is unchanged at $18.4m. At $2.93/bottle the company hits zero profit. Candidate should also note that $1/bottle costs $7m, reducing profit to $13.5m. Strong answer also discusses qualitative considerations: slim margins on standard wines, reputational upside, possible distributor reimbursement.

math.setup: Total bottles = 1m + 2m + 4m = 7m. Profit at rate r = $55m – r x 7m – $34.5m (no more refund losses). Breakeven with current fakes scenario: r x 7m = $2.1m. Breakeven with zero profit: $55m – r x 7m – $34.5m = 0 → r x 7m = $20.5m.
steps: To match current net profit of $18.4m: screening cost = $2.1m → $2.1m / 7m = $0.30/bottle
math.answer: Maximum willingness to pay to break even vs. zero profit: ~$2.93/bottle. To maintain current profit level: $0.30/bottle.

recommendation: ALSH should partner with a third-party screener to filter out fake wines before they are sold to customers, and should aim to pay around $0.30 per bottle screened.
risks: Depending on the price paid, screening can be extremely expensive and further cut into profitability.
Demand for ALSH's services may take time to rebound as customers remain apprehensive.
Third-party screeners may not be 100% accurate in detecting fakes.
next_steps: ALSH should launch an advertising campaign to announce its efforts to combat selling fake wines.
ALSH may consider selling more expensive wines given the added screening, positioning it as a premium service.
ALSH may consider reducing refunds on standard sizes where the refund cost ($200) exceeds the bottle price ($30); changing refund policy would alter the screening economics.
ALSH should explore whether the wine distributor can reimburse screening costs when fakes are found.
